title: Korean grammar
intro: A working reference for beginners to intermediate learners. Korean puts the verb last and marks each word's role with a particle after it. Read a section, notice the shape, then listen for it in what you watch and read.

sections.title: Word order & particles
sections.text: The basic order is **subject – object – verb**, and the verb always comes last. Because particles show the roles, the other words can move, and anything obvious from context is left out: **먹었어요?** (Did [you] eat?) is a full sentence. **은/는** marks the topic or a contrast; **이/가** marks the subject, often new information.

head: Particle
After a vowel / consonant
Role
Example
rows: at a time, to a place, existence
학교에 가요. | I go to school.
도서관에서 공부해요. | I study at the library.

examples.translation: At the weekend I exercise in the park.
examples.note: 에 for time, 에서 for the place of action

sections.title: To be (이다, 아니다, 있다, 없다)
sections.text: **이다** links two nouns and attaches to the noun: 예요 after a vowel, 이에요 after a consonant. **있다 / 없다** mean both "there is / isn't" and "to have / not have", and also location: **화장실이 어디에 있어요?** (Where is the toilet?).

head: Meaning
Form
Example
rows: 의사예요. | (I'm) a doctor. ;; 학생이에요. | (I'm) a student.
돈이 없어요. | I have no money.

examples.translation: Do you have a younger sibling?

sections.title: Speech levels (해요, 합니다, 해)
sections.text: Start with **해요체**: it's polite and safe almost everywhere. You'll hear **합니다체** on the news and in shops (**감사합니다**), and **반말** among friends in dramas. The honorific **-(으)시-** raises the person you talk about: **선생님이 오세요** (The teacher is coming).

sections.title: Present tense (-아요 / -어요)
sections.rule: Drop -다. If the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ add -아요; otherwise -어요; 하다 becomes 해요.
sections.text: Verbs don't change for person: **가요** = I / you / he / they go. Vowels merge: 가 + 아 → 가, 보 + 아 → 봐, 마시 + 어 → 마셔. Adjectives conjugate like verbs: **좋다 → 좋아요** (it's good), **맛있다 → 맛있어요** (it's tasty). A rising voice turns any statement into a question.

sections.title: Past (-았/었-) & future (-ㄹ 거예요)
sections.text: **-(으)ㄹ 거예요** is the general future and also a guess (**비가 올 거예요**, it'll probably rain). **-(으)ㄹ게요** is a promise to the listener.

head: Rule
Examples
rows: stem + 았어요 / 었어요 / 했어요 (same vowel rule)
갔어요 | went ;; 먹었어요 | ate ;; 공부했어요 | studied
갈 거예요 | will go ;; 먹을 거예요 | will eat

sections.title: Negation (안, 못, -지 않다)
sections.text: **안** goes right before the verb (inside 하다 verbs: 공부 안 해요); **못** means "can't". The long forms with **-지 않다 / -지 못하다** sound a little more formal and are common in writing.

sections.title: Linking clauses (-고, -지만, -아서, -(으)니까)
sections.text: Korean links clauses by changing the ending of the first verb; only the last verb carries tense and politeness. With -아서/어서 don't add past tense to the first verb: **늦어서 미안해요** (Sorry I'm / I was late).

head: Ending
Meaning
Example
rows: 밥을 먹고 학교에 가요. | I eat and go to school.
비싸지만 맛있어요. | It's expensive but tasty.
피곤해서 일찍 잤어요. | I was tired so I slept early.
시간이 있으면 같이 가요. | If you have time, let's go together.

examples.translation: I was hungry, so I made ramen.
If you're tired, rest a bit.

sections.title: Want, can, have to, try
sections.text: These are some of the most frequent endings in speech: learn them as chunks. **-(으)세요** is the polite request you hear constantly (**잠깐만 기다리세요**, please wait a moment).

head: Meaning
Pattern
Example
rows: 한국에 가고 싶어요. | I want to go to Korea.
수영할 수 있어요. | I can swim.
일찍 일어나야 해요. | I have to get up early.

examples.translation: What do you want to eat?
I have to finish by tomorrow.

sections.title: Describing nouns (-(으)ㄴ, -는, -(으)ㄹ)
sections.text: Everything describing a noun comes **before** it, including whole clauses, so "the book that I read yesterday" is **어제 읽은 책** (yesterday read book). Listen for the ending just before the noun: it tells you the time.

head: Ending
Example
rows: 큰 집 | a big house ;; 좋은 사람 | a good person
먹는 음식 | food (people) eat ;; 일하는 사람 | a person who works
어제 본 영화 | the film (I) saw yesterday
내일 할 일 | the work to do tomorrow

examples.translation: What's the name of the person you met yesterday?

sections.title: Two number systems
sections.text: Time mixes both: **세 시 이십 분** (3:20, native hours + Sino minutes). Counted things take a counter: **사과 두 개** (two apples), **사람 세 명** (three people), **책 한 권** (one book).

head: Native Korean
Sino-Korean
rows: counting things and people, hours, age
dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors

examples.text: 지금 몇 시예요? 두 시 반이에요.
examples.translation: What time is it? It's half past two.
How much is this? It's 15,000 won.

sections.title: One-page memory map
points: The verb comes last; particles after each word show its role.
은/는 = topic or contrast; 이/가 = subject; 을/를 = object.
에 = to / at (time, destination); 에서 = where the action happens.
Polite present: stem + 아요 / 어요 / 해요; the form doesn't change for person.
Past: 았어요 / 었어요 / 했어요; future: (으)ㄹ 거예요.
Describing words and clauses go before the noun: 어제 본 영화.
Native numbers count things and hours; Sino numbers for money, dates, minutes.
sections.tip: Listening strategy: wait for the end of the sentence: the final verb carries the meaning, the tense and the politeness. Particles are short and often dropped in speech, so lean on word order and context.
